title: Rat Mothers Who Lick Their Pups
text:
At McGill University in Montreal, Michael Meaney and his colleagues had noticed that rat mothers differ in how they care for their newborn pups. Some spend a lot of time licking and grooming them and nursing in an arched-back posture; others do much less. The pups of attentive mothers grew into calmer adults, less fearful and with milder hormonal responses to stress.

But was that inherited or learned from care? The researchers swapped litters at birth, so that pups born to low-licking mothers were raised by high-licking ones and the reverse. The pups grew up to resemble their foster mothers, not their birth mothers. The care itself was making the difference.

In 2004, Ian Weaver, Meaney and colleagues showed one way it worked. In the brain region called the hippocampus, they examined a gene that helps control the stress response by producing receptors for stress hormones. In pups of high-licking mothers, chemical tags known as methyl groups were less present on a key switch region of this gene, so it was more active. These differences appeared in the first week of life and lasted into adulthood. When the researchers treated adult rats with a drug that affects these chemical marks, the differences could be partly reversed.

The study became a founding example of how early experience can leave lasting marks on how genes are used.
lesson: Early care can shape how a body handles stress for a lifetime. Tenderness toward the very young is not sentimentality; it builds resilience.
people: Ian Weaver, Michael Meaney and colleagues
source: Weaver, I. C. G., Cervoni, N., Champagne, F. A., D'Alessio, A. C., Sharma, S., Seckl, J. R., Dymov, S., Szyf, M., and Meaney, M. J. (2004). Epigenetic programming by maternal behavior. Nature Neuroscience, 7(8), 847-854.
caveat: The findings come from rats, and how far they apply to human parenting is still uncertain.
